blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical scalability problem in modern spreadsheet systems like Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice Calc. Despite claiming support for millions of cells, these systems struggle with datasets far below their advertised limits, often freezing or becoming unusable. The paper introduces two benchmark suites: Basic Complexity Testing (BCT) to analyze time complexity of operations and identify when interactivity breaks (defined as response times exceeding 500ms), and Optimization Opportunities Testing (OOT) to probe for database-like optimizations such as indexing, incremental updates, and columnar layouts. The findings reveal widespread inefficiencies—spreadsheets fail to employ common database techniques, leading to poor performance on operations like sorting, filtering, and VLOOKUPs. The author emphasizes the need to apply database principles to spreadsheet systems to improve scalability and interactivity.
paper_abstract: 14–19, 2020, Portland, OR, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 11 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3318464.3389782 Spreadsheet systems are used for storing and analyzing data across domains by programmers and non-programmers alike. While spreadsheet systems have continued to support increasingly large datasets, they are prone to hanging and freezing while performing computations even on much smaller ones. We present a benchmarking study that evaluates and compares the performance of three popular systems, Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc, and Google Sheets, on a range of canonical spreadsheet computation operations. We find that spreadsheet systems lack interactivity for several operations, on datasets well below their advertised scalability limits. We further evaluate whether spreadsheet systems adopt database optimization techniques such as indexing, intelligent data layout, and incremental and shared computation, to efficiently execute computation operations. We outline several ways future spreadsheet systems can be redesigned to offer interactive response times on large datasets.
